text: A dedicated radio frequency is used for the duration of the crane operations, and the crane operator normally takes radio instructions from one person only.
Only one dogger gives signals at any time. Where more than one dogger is involved in a lift, each knows when responsibility for their part of the lift is handed over.
Work stops immediately if radio communication is lost. Mobile phones are not used to direct tower crane operations.
An anemometer is fixed on the tower crane where it is not shielded from the wind, to give an accurate wind speed reading.
The crane is not operated in wind speeds above 54 km/h unless it is designed for those conditions and a documented risk assessment sets the types of loads that can be lifted and the controls.
Workers, the tower crane and its load stay at least 3 m from overhead powerlines up to 132 kV, with greater distances for higher voltages. Allow for load overshoot and for sway and sag of the lines.

Where the crane or load could enter the powerline exclusion zone, a trained safety observer (spotter) watches and advises the operator. The safety observer does not carry out dogging or other tasks at the same time.
There is at least 2 m between the highest point of the building work and the bottom of a slung load, unless not reasonably practicable.

Where a concrete placement boom works within the tower crane's operating radius, a documented procedure sets the siting, communication between operators and scheduling, and the crane boom stays an appropriate distance above the placement boom.
The crane operator does not do their own dogging (for example on a remote control tower crane) or supervise a trainee dogger, even if the operator holds a dogging licence.
On a self-erecting or remotely operated crane, the operator works from a designated area close to the crane, keeps the load in view, and stays stationary while the load is in motion.
If the remote control operator needs to do other tasks, the remote control is turned off and secured so it cannot be activated unintentionally or used by others.
A barricade about 1800 mm high (for example a mesh fence) is erected around the base of a self-erecting tower crane, with room to avoid entrapment between the barricade and the counterweights.

Before each work shift the crane operator visually inspects and function tests the crane, including controls, brakes, limiting devices and wire ropes, and enters the results in the logbook kept with the crane. Faults are fixed before use.

step: Rig, lift and land loads with the tower crane
text: Before directing a lift, the dogger checks each sling, shackle and lifting attachment has a working load limit at least equal to the load, the load is balanced, no part is loose, and it is not snagged.

step: Rig, lift and land loads with the tower crane
text: Lifting hooks have operable safety latches, shackles are prevented from unscrewing (for example by mousing), and slings are protected from sharp edges with sleeves or corner pieces.

step: Rig, lift and land loads with the tower crane
text: Round (sausage) slings are used only for round loads, as sharp edged loads can damage or tear them.

step: Rig, lift and land loads with the tower crane
text: Lifting gear is inspected by a competent person at least every 12 months, and synthetic slings every 3 months, and is tagged with the date of its last inspection.

step: Rig, lift and land loads with the tower crane
text: When handling maximum or near maximum loads, after lifting the load a few centimetres the operator tests the hoist brakes, checks the load indicator and rechecks the load chart.

step: Rig, lift and land loads with the tower crane
text: Except in an emergency, the crane operator does not leave the cabin or control room while a load is suspended from the crane.

step: Rig, lift and land loads with the tower crane
text: Material boxes are engineer designed and certified, marked with their tare mass and SWL, lifted on four chains, with loads secured and not stacked above the sides.

step: Rig, lift and land loads with the tower crane
text: Basket hitches are not used where people may be near a lifted load, unless the sling is positively restrained from sliding along the load.

step: Rig, lift and land loads with the tower crane
text: Avoid lifting multiple loads at the same time (high/low loads), as it is difficult to ensure the dogger is not underneath them.

step: Rig, lift and land loads with the tower crane
text: The crane is not left unattended until all loads are removed from the hook, the hook is raised clear, all powered motions are disabled, the keys are removed, and access to the crane base is prevented.

step: Erect or dismantle the tower crane
text: Before erecting or dismantling starts, an exclusion zone based on a risk assessment is set up, including where practicable a radius of at least 20 m from the crane base. Only persons involved in the work enter it.

step: Erect or dismantle the tower crane
text: Before climbing the crane, an exclusion zone with a radius of at least 12 m from the crane base is set up where practicable, and no one enters the area behind the crane under the counterweights.

step: Erect or dismantle the tower crane
text: Climbing is not attempted at wind speeds above 36 km/h, or if the recommended maximum or actual wind speed is unknown.

step: Erect or dismantle the tower crane
text: No slewing during climbing. The counterweight trolleys, including side plates, bolting, pins, safety gear, ropes and turnbuckles, are inspected before climbing starts.

step: Erect or dismantle the tower crane
text: Tower sections are of the correct model, or a model of greater strength, and the same as those on the engineer's crane base drawing.

step: Erect or dismantle the tower crane
text: Only the correct type and grade of tower bolts are used, bolts and pins are not defective, and tower bolts are correctly torqued, neither under nor over tightened.

step: Erect or dismantle the tower crane
text: Crane components such as packers and shims are restrained from falling, for example with a short chain to the crane structure, and tool lanyards at the wrist are no longer than 300 mm.

step: Erect or dismantle the tower crane
text: Rated capacity limiters, overload cut-outs or motion switches bypassed or disconnected during erection are reconnected and tested to a written procedure before the crane is put into operation.

step: Erect or dismantle the tower crane
text: Edge protection or travel restraint is used where it can be installed. A fall-arrest harness is used only where these are not practicable, with a written procedure for retrieving a person after a fall.

step: Set up the concrete pump and placing boom
text: Outrigger timbers have a minimum width of 200 mm and thickness of 75 mm, laid together with no gaps so the timber pad is wider than the outrigger foot, unless the manufacturer specifies otherwise.

step: Set up the concrete pump and placing boom
text: On sloping ground, cut into the ground so outrigger timbers are set level. Timbers are not laid on the slope or placed over timbers underneath.

step: Set up the concrete pump and placing boom
text: When unfolding the boom, test stability by slowly slewing the extended boom over each outrigger. If an outrigger sinks, slew back, fold the boom and adjust the dunnage before repeating.

step: Set up the concrete pump and placing boom
text: Vertical pipelines are positively secured to the building, and the 90 degree bend at the base is securely supported. Cranes, hoist towers, scaffolding or formwork are not used to secure the line.

step: Set up the concrete pump and placing boom
text: Anchor brackets and tie-downs secure the pipeline at intervals of no more than 3 m, unless a competent person specifies otherwise.

step: Set up the concrete pump and placing boom
text: Pipe clamps can sustain the maximum concrete pressure, locking pins on quick release clamps are engaged, the correct gasket is fitted, and clamps are not locked by hammering the lever. Damaged clamps are replaced immediately.

step: Set up the concrete pump and placing boom
text: The safety observer (spotter) for powerlines does not carry out other work at the same time, observes only one item of plant, and has the authority to stop the concrete placing equipment.

step: Set up the concrete pump and placing boom
text: Short legging is used only where the manufacturer's operating manual permits it, under a documented safe work procedure with a diagram of the permissible operating zone of the boom, given to the principal contractor.
Provide one line hand for every 10 m of workable hose where the pipe diameter is 76.2 mm or more, and every 20 m where it is less.
The delivery hose on a boom pump hangs close to vertical and is guided only by the line hand. If the boom does not reach, use a longer boom or move the pump closer.
The line hand has a working surface at least 450 mm wide to stand on, and does not stand on block walls or next to unprotected edges.
No person stands between a reversing concrete delivery truck and the hopper, and the truck stops immediately if the driver loses sight of the spotter.
The truck's concrete chute is moved only when the truck is stationary, preferably by the driver or with the driver's permission.
Concrete is pumped only when the hopper grate is closed.
Where a worker must enter the hopper for cleaning, the equipment is shut down and accumulated hydraulic or air pressure exhausted, with another person nearby to assist.
Compressed air is not used to clear a suspected blockage. When blowing out a line with air, remove the rubber delivery hose and reducers, secure the line end, and fit a catchment device.
For air cleanout, the blowout cap has a pressure gauge and an air dump valve, and only experienced, authorised workers operate its valves.
Confirm the mix delivered matches the mix ordered. The person at the hopper monitors the mix and has the pump operator do an emergency stop if lumps or foreign objects appear.
Where concrete is pumped by hose, provide one line hand for every 10 m of workable hose where the pipe diameter is 76.2 mm or more, and every 20 m where it is less.
Where concrete is pumped, no person stands between a reversing delivery truck and the hopper, and the truck stops immediately if the driver loses sight of the spotter.
The line hand has a working surface at least 450 mm wide to stand on, and does not stand on wall tops or next to unprotected edges.

step: Erect and connect steel at height
text: Columns are secured by bolting the base plate to the footing, with tightly fitted steel packers or wedges under the base plate, and are stabilised against overturning before the lifting gear is released.

step: Erect and connect steel at height
text: Where possible, lifting slings are released from floor level using long slings or remote release shackles, or from an EWP.

step: Erect and connect steel at height
text: All beams are secured before the slings are released.

step: Erect and connect steel at height
text: Bolts are not bent and holes are not enlarged to line up. Where holes do not line up, the design engineer is consulted and gives written verification of any changes.

step: Erect and connect steel at height
text: Where the design requires, erection starts in a nominated braced bay so the structure can be plumbed and made self-supporting.

step: Erect and connect steel at height
text: Temporary guys and bracing are securely anchored, identified with coloured bunting, and inspected at the beginning of each shift. Any anchor movement is reported to the erector and acted on immediately.

step: Erect and connect steel at height

step: Erect and connect steel at height

step: Erect and connect steel at height

step: Erect and connect steel at height

step: Erect and connect steel at height

step: Lift and land steel with the crane company
text: Take care when releasing strapping on steel bundles, as the strapping may whip back or the bundle may fall apart.

step: Lift and land steel with the crane company

step: Lift and land steel with the crane company
text: Steelwork is stored in stable stacks so it cannot fall on workers, allowing for wind and mobile plant, with safe access for workers to sling a load.

step: Lift and land steel with the crane company

step: Lift and land steel with the crane company
text: Only one person gives signals at any one time, and work stops immediately if 2-way radio contact is lost.

step: Lift and land steel with the crane company
text: The crane operator gives an audible warning before lifting loads near persons.
Where the lift is not designed by an engineer, each crane's capacity is at least 20% greater than its calculated share of the load for two cranes, 33% for three, and 50% for four.
One person is in overall control of the multiple crane lift, cranes of equal capacity and similar characteristics are used, and the lift is rehearsed wherever possible.
Outrigger extensions are locked or pinned as the manufacturer recommends, and pads sit on hardwood packing at least 200 x 75 mm laid in a pigsty configuration, not parallel. The crane is levelled.
The outrigger footings are checked frequently during the crane's operation to make sure they stay in place.
When handling maximum or near maximum loads, after lifting the load a few centimetres test the hoist brakes, check the load weight indicator and recheck the load chart.
When travelling with a load, keep it close to the ground, with a dogger who stays in sight of the operator and out of the crane's path, and the slewing brake or lock applied.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: An exclusion zone, with para-webbing, signs or fencing as needed, keeps out everyone not involved in erection and covers the area where a falling crane, panel or struck element could hit a person.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: The exclusion zone stays in place until the braces are secured and the lifting slings removed, and traffic is stopped from passing through it during lifting.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: The semi-trailer is unloaded on firm, level ground with a side slope of no more than 2 degrees, wheels chocked and park brake on, and is never moved after the restraints are released.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: Panels are unloaded progressively from alternate sides of the A-frame so trailer tilt is kept to a minimum, and no one stands beside the vehicle where a panel could strike them.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: The dogger slings panels on the trailer from a work platform, such as a guarded A-frame walkway, boom EWP, mobile scaffold or loading bay, or uses pre-attached slings reached from the ground, not from a ladder.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: Before lifting, the panel mass is clearly marked on the panel, and the crane capacity covers the panel, lifting gear and dynamic factors at the actual working radius.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: Crane support is maintained until all braces are installed and secured to the panel and footings, without the hoist rope or slings going slack.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: Lifting clutch release lines are fitted so clutches can be released without workers climbing on top of the panel.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: Dowel pins are fitted before lowering, and levelling shims do not exceed 40 mm in height.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: Tilt-up panels are lifted only when documentation verifies the concrete has reached the minimum strength required for the lifting inserts.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: If a tilt-up panel does not come free when the crane indicator shows the combined weight of panel and rigging, lifting stops. Wedging or jacking needs the engineer's approval. Panels lean away from the crane, never towards it.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: Braces are inspected before use, marked with the manufacturer's name, model and working load limit, and do not have parts interchanged with other makes or models.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: Brace locking pins have retaining devices, and knee or lateral bracing is installed as soon as possible after the panel is placed and the primary braces are secured.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: Deformation-controlled expansion anchors, drop-in anchors, low-load slip (wedge) anchors and self-drilling anchors are not used for braces. Chemical anchors are used only if each is proof tested to its working load limit.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: Post-installed brace anchors are torqued with a torque wrench or calibrated rattle gun, and written records of setting torque are kept on site.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: Mobile plant does not operate or travel close to erected panels and braces unless there is good reason, and must never contact a brace. Brace positions are marked with hazard tape, para-webbing or signs.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: A lift plan shows crane set-up positions, lift locations and radius, obstacles in the slew path, and areas such as trenches and covered penetrations where the crane cannot set up.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: A crane on outriggers is level to within 1 degree, on correctly pig-stied timbers of the manufacturer's minimum size, and not next to excavations or over covered cavities.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: Where the ground slope is greater than 1 degree, written evidence is provided that the crane can safely walk a load on that gradient.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: Lifting of concrete elements does not continue when the wind speed exceeds 45 km/h (12.5 m/s), and lower speeds may be unsafe for elements with a large surface area.

step: Stand and brace the precast elements
text: Stored panels are stable in wind, on at least two bearers aligned through the stack, stacked no higher than twice the element width, away from roads, and on a suspended slab only with the slab engineer's written approval.
Braces are removed from platforms with edge protection, such as EWPs or mobile scaffolds. A ladder is used only to undo the bolt on a light brace that workers on the ground lower in a controlled way.

text: The surface is checked for asbestos before blasting. Compressed air and high pressure water are never used on asbestos or asbestos-containing material.

Low-dust abrasives, such as chilled iron grit or cast steel grit, are used where reasonably practicable. The label and SDS are checked for impurities, and abrasives above 1 Bq/g radiation are not used.
Small items are blasted in a blasting cabinet and transportable items in a blasting chamber. Fixed structures are blasted inside a temporary enclosure with dust extraction fitted.

Temporary enclosure screens are puncture- and tear-resistant. Shadecloth or other porous material is not used where the work generates silica, lead or other toxic dust. Where full enclosure is not possible, screening extends 2 m above the structure and blasting is directed downwards.

An exclusion zone, sized by risk assessment and extended downwind, keeps out anyone not wearing RPE. Signs visible before entry say blasting is in progress, there is a dust hazard, access is for authorised persons only and RPE must be worn.
Blasting stops in windy conditions, and other work is stopped and people are cleared from the area while blasting takes place.

Breathing air to blast helmets is of adequate quality, the compressor air intake is well away from engine exhausts, air-fed respirators have a carbon monoxide alarm, and air lines are protected from vehicles and the blasting.
The pot attendant and anyone else in the work area wear an air purifying respirator during blasting, maintenance, repair and dust clean-up.

Blasters also wear a protective suit closed at the wrists and ankles, canvas or leather gloves and protective footwear. The helmet cape is replaced immediately if damaged and never repaired with tape.
The nozzle is pointed only at the work, never at a person, and blasting is never done with a coiled hose.
The dead man control is inspected and tested several times each working day, and the operator checks the blasting plant daily for wear and damage before use.

Blast hoses are anti-static or earthed, within their rated working pressure and kept as straight as possible. Pin holes are never taped, hoses with a damaged cover are replaced, and elevated hoses are supported by safety cables.
In dry blasting, the nozzle and the object being blasted are earthed to discharge static electricity.
The compressor or air supply has a safety relief valve, blast pots have a muffler, and the rated working pressure is never exceeded.
A dedicated pot attendant keeps the blaster in sight to give help if needed.
Spent abrasive and dust are collected by vacuum recovery or wet methods, never by sweeping or compressed air blowdown, and waste is covered so it cannot become airborne.
Abrasive used on concrete, sandstone or other silica-bearing surfaces is not recycled unless its crystalline silica content is shown to remain below the allowed amount.
Blasters shower and change after blasting, wash hands and face before eating or drinking, and eat in a clean area separate from the blast site.
Blast helmets have air cooling devices where heat is a risk, cool drinking water is readily available, and rest breaks are taken in a cool, well-ventilated area.
Time on the nozzle is limited by job rotation or more frequent breaks to reduce hand-arm vibration.

text: Surfaces are checked for asbestos before water blasting. High pressure water is never used on asbestos or asbestos-containing material.
Outside a spray booth, a spray painting exclusion zone is set by risk assessment, generally at least 3 m in all directions horizontally and 2 m above and below the spraying, and larger in stairwells.
The exclusion zone has physical barriers and a sign saying 'SPRAY PAINTING AREA - AUTHORISED PERSONNEL ONLY'. No one else enters during spraying unless wearing the same PPE as the sprayer.
Only the spray gun and its cables are in the exclusion zone. Other electrical equipment is outside it, enclosed in a fire-resistant structure, or certified for explosive atmospheres.
The spray area is shrouded to stop drift reaching walkways, public areas and air conditioning intakes, and spraying stops when wind is likely to spread drift.

Indoors, spraying is done in open construction or with mechanical exhaust or local exhaust ventilation to stop flammable or toxic fumes building up. High hazard paints are not sprayed indoors without exhaust ventilation.

Drums of paint and cleaning solvent not needed are removed from the exclusion zone before spraying, and solvent-soaked rags and waste paint are removed promptly. A suitable fire extinguisher is readily available.
A spanner is used to tighten the tip guard or clear a blocked reversible tip. The gun is never cleaned by covering the nozzle with a cloth held in the hand.
The sprayer wears full length overalls with hood, chemically resistant gloves and eye protection.

Changing, washing and eating areas are kept separate from the spray zone.

text: Material that may be asbestos is either assumed to be asbestos or sampled by a competent person and analysed by a NATA-accredited laboratory, or one approved or operated by the regulator. Samples are sealed and double bagged.
Where asbestos is present, the work is planned so it is not disturbed, for example by routing wiring over an asbestos wall or running a flue through a non-asbestos wall.
Asbestos components are replaced only with non-asbestos products. Asbestos is never reinstalled or reused.

text: Floors and other surfaces that could become contaminated are covered with heavy duty 200 µm plastic sheeting secured with cloth or duct tape.
Decontamination facilities for workers, equipment and items worked on are set up before work starts, and anything leaving the work area is decontaminated first.
Only a HEPA filtered H class industrial vacuum cleaner is used. Household vacuum cleaners are never used where asbestos is or may be present, even with a HEPA filter.
Work is not done in windy conditions that could spread asbestos fibres, and as few people as possible are present.

find: Isolate the area with barriers and asbestos warning signs.

text: Asbestos is wetted with a surfactant or wetting agent, such as detergent water. Before water is used, the work is checked for electrical hazards, and where one exists the hazard is dealt with rather than working dry.
Disposable coveralls are type 5, category 3, with fitted hoods worn over respirator straps and cuffs taped. No open pockets or velcro. Laceless boots, such as gumboots, are worn.
Respirators stay on until coveralls are vacuumed or removed inside out and bagged, and personal washing, including hands and fingernails, is done.
Clothing worn under coveralls is disposed of or bagged for laundering as asbestos-contaminated clothing, and is never laundered at home.

find: Keep the material wet and remove it whole, by hand.

step: Bag, label and dispose of asbestos waste
text: Waste goes in 200 µm polyethylene bags labelled 'Danger Asbestos - Do not open or damage bag. Do not inhale dust', each sealed with tape and placed in a second bag. Bag surfaces are wet wiped before leaving the work area.

step: Bag, label and dispose of asbestos waste
text: Waste awaiting disposal is kept in closed containers, such as lined steel drums with lids or a sealed skip, and never put in the general waste.

find: Wrap the waste in heavy duty plastic, label it as asbestos waste and take it to a facility licensed to accept it.

text: On an asbestos cement roof, no pressure cleaner or blower is used. Debris is wetted with detergent water from a watering can or garden sprayer, without making a slurry, and removed with a scoop or trowel.
On an asbestos cement roof, downpipes are disconnected or re-routed so contaminated water cannot enter the waste water system, and runoff is collected and disposed of as asbestos waste.
Debris from an asbestos cement roof goes straight into labelled heavy duty asbestos waste bags. Workers wear disposable coveralls and at least a P1 or P2 half face respirator.

step: Remove the old board and fit the new one

Stepladders and trestle ladders are not used to get onto the roof. A single or extension ladder is used only where a scaffold stair, fixed ladder or other safer access is not reasonably practicable.

Where an EWP is used to reach the roof, workers leave the basket only by the procedure in AS 2550.10, at a gated opening in the edge protection, with the EWP in a barricaded bay clear of other moving plant.
Before temporary edge protection is installed, the building structure is assessed, with the roof design engineer where needed, to confirm it can support the loads the guardrail system imposes.
Edge protection is installed from the ground, from an EWP, or pre-fixed to structural members where reasonably practicable, to minimise work at height.
As fascias, gutters and cladding are added or removed, the gaps between rails and between the bottom rail and the roof edge are checked and the edge protection is adjusted.
Where a catch platform is part of scaffold edge protection, it is as close as practicable to the underside of the roof and no lower than 1 m below the roof edge.

Covers over openings and non-trafficable surfaces are securely fixed against dislodgement, designed for a concentrated load of at least 2 kN, and clearly distinguishable from roofing material so they are not removed as waste.
Roof safety mesh is installed by a competent person to AS/NZS 4389, full length gutter to gutter where practicable, and is not walked on unless it is designed for that purpose.
Roof safety mesh is run out using pull lines or similar techniques so installers minimise work at height.

Roof trusses, steel beams or other structure are used as anchorage points only once a competent person verifies they can take fall-arrest loads. Temporarily braced or incomplete structural members are never used as anchorages.

Where the anchor is on the roof surface, it is as far behind the worker as practicable, the worker stays close to directly in front of it, and the lanyard is the shortest length needed, to limit swing falls and free fall.

Standard inertia reels (SRLs) are used only anchored above the user with the line close to vertical, unless the manufacturer permits horizontal use. Leading edge SRLs are used for foot-level anchorages.
A total restraint system uses a prescribed lanyard length so workers cannot reach an edge, hole or fragile surface, and workers do not swap in their own longer lanyards.
Each worker inspects their harness, lanyard and connectors for wear and damage before and after use, and after storage or transport.

text: Where edge protection is removed to install a hoist, tile elevator or other lifting equipment, alternative fall protection is provided, and the removed parts are replaced as soon as the equipment is installed or no longer needed.

text: Tile elevator and builders' hoist drives and belt nip points are guarded, and barricades keep people away from moving parts and from the area where objects could fall.

text: Storage and landing areas on the roof are designated after the roof structure is assessed for load capacity, so the roof is not overloaded.

text: Where sheets are slid onto the roof under the toe board or infill panel, the gap is controlled so tools and materials cannot fall through it.

Work across the roof is sequenced to minimise the number of leading edges, with a roof cladding installer only work zone marked 6 m back from each leading edge and roof access limited to workers directly involved.
Wear footwear with good grip on sloped or uneven roof surfaces, and knee pads when kneeling or crouching.
Stepladders and trestle ladders are not used to get onto the roof. A single or extension ladder is used only where a scaffold stair, fixed ladder or other safer access is not reasonably practicable.

Before work starts on an existing roof, a competent person inspects it for the presence and condition of safety mesh, the roof's structural integrity, fragile sheets and skylights, and asbestos, electrical and radio frequency hazards.

Before going onto a roof with radio transmitting antennas, the building manager is consulted and the site's EME guide obtained. Workers stay out of its exclusion zones unless transmitter power reduction or shutdown has been arranged and verified.
No one works alone on the roof without a check-in system: contact at set times, an emergency response if they fail to report in, and a phone or radio to call for help at any time.

Covers over openings and non-trafficable surfaces are securely fixed against dislodgement, designed for a concentrated load of at least 2 kN, and clearly distinguishable from roofing material so they are not removed as waste.
Existing roof safety mesh is relied on only after a competent person has inspected it and confirmed the integrity of the mesh and its supporting members.
Sacrificial edge protection brackets left from earlier work are assessed by a competent person, with their fixings, before they are reused.
Where a no-go area is used, it is marked by a barricade that gives a visual and physical warning, set at least 3 m from any fall hazard on a flat trafficable roof, with signs.

Where only a defined zone of a low-pitch roof (under 7 degrees) is accessed, temporary edge protection extends at least 3 m beyond each side of the work zone, and the rest of the roof is a marked no-go area.
Asbestos cement roofing is never water blasted or cleaned with compressed air.

step: Install plant and equipment on the roof
text: Temporary edge protection is provided wherever a fall hazard is within 3 m of the work zone around the plant.
Consumer mains and solar panel cables running through the roof space are treated as energised even when the main switch is off.

Skylights, roof openings and any fragile surface are covered with fixed covers that take a fall, or fenced off, before work starts near them.

The harness system is set up so free fall is no more than 2 m before it takes effect
Exclusion zone below the lift and below the roof edge, with barriers and signs.

Secure sheets and offcuts stacked on the roof against wind, and do not stack them near unprotected edges

Cover or barricade openings as soon as sheets are removed.

text: No part of the gantry is within 4 m of a power line unless the electricity network operator approves a lesser distance. Long components are handled so they cannot enter the approach distance.

Barriers such as concrete or metal barriers, buffer rails or rated water-filled barriers protect the gantry from vehicle impact, as the design engineer advises, particularly near intersections and on bends.
At least 2.2 m of clear headroom is kept above the footway to bracing, beams and every other part of the gantry.
The gantry is not connected to the facade or cladding of the building unless it is designed as a dual-purpose structure.
Any change to the gantry is recorded by the installer and referred to the designer to update and re-certify the design.
Materials stored on the deck stay within the load the engineer sets, for a 10 kPa gantry typically no more than 40 per cent of the design live load.
Where people have access to the deck, it has edge protection at least 900 mm high to AS 4994, a slip-resistant surface, and a perimeter enclosed so objects cannot fall.
The site boundary under the gantry is fenced to stop unauthorised access, and the deck is waterproofed and drained as the design sets out.
Lighting wiring is not tied in with permanent wiring or fixed to freestanding fences, and is protected in conduit or armoured cable, with light fittings protected by diffusers.

The site supervisor checks the gantry daily for damage, overloading, movement or over-stacking. A competent person inspects it after installation and any damaging event, and at least every 6 months, or every 30 days for a scaffold gantry.
Vehicle access points under the gantry have the height clearance signed, with clear driver sightlines.
Pedestrians are protected when concrete boom trucks, cranes or concrete pump static lines are used along the gantry frontage.

Sheds, containers and toilets on a gantry are fixed as the engineer advises so they cannot move. Where crane loads pass over them, their roofs or a secondary structure are rated the same as the gantry.
Sheds and materials on a gantry deck leave clear emergency egress routes, including for a stretcher from any first aid room on the deck.

find: Sheds on a gantry go only where the engineer's design allows for their load.
Get the current underground services information before digging or driving footings for fences, hoardings and gantries

text: Before each use, the operator does a pre-operational inspection and function test to the manufacturer's instructions, including emergency lowering, controls, gate, guardrails, tyres, outriggers and logbook. A faulty EWP is not used, and is locked out and tagged.

Workers on the ground and on the platform, including spotters and safety observers, are trained to use the emergency lowering controls. The EWP is positioned so they stay accessible from the ground, and the lowering path is kept clear.
Where remote or portable controls are used, their orientation is checked before the EWP is moved so the operator knows which way it will move.
Workers enter and leave the platform only through the gate with the platform lowered, and keep the gate latched. No one climbs on the guardrails or uses ladders on the platform to gain height.
The lanyard is as short as possible, has a personal energy absorber, and is attached only to the designated anchor point.

Outriggers are set to the manufacturer's instructions before the platform is raised, with spreader plates, pads or mats under them, footplates are never set on a slope, and the EWP is not moved with the outriggers extended.
The EWP works within the maximum slope on its manufacturer's plate. Where it is set up on a slope, the braked wheels face up the incline.
The operator checks the ground for a firm crust over soft ground, water, backfilled trenches and covered cavities, and checks that pads have not sunk where the EWP works in one spot for a long time.

Before travelling, the boom is retracted and the platform lowered where possible, the travel path is clear, a spotter is used on slopes and in congested areas, and no one rides the platform unless the manufacturer allows it.
If the EWP starts to tilt, work stops and the platform is lowered or retracted. Work does not restart until the cause is found and fixed, with a competent person's advice where needed.
Wind is monitored on site with an anemometer or manufacturer-approved method, and the wind limit is derated for signs, mesh or other attachments that add sail area.
Barricades keep other workers, plant and the public clear of the EWP's operating area and where objects could fall, and only the operator and people directly involved are near it.
Near traffic, the boom's pivot point and reach are set so it cannot extend into live lanes, under a traffic management plan with barricaded exclusion zones.
Tools are secured to an anchor point with tool lanyards so they cannot fall from the platform.
Where the EWP could enter Zone B of a power line, the work is authorised by the electricity supply authority, and a trained safety observer marks Zone B, watches only that EWP and can stop the work.

If the EWP contacts a power line, stay on the platform until a competent person says it is safe. If you must leave, lower it, jump clear without touching the EWP and ground together, and shuffle away. Keep everyone clear.
After contact with a power line, the EWP is out of service until a competent person inspects it. An EWP with inflatable tyres is kept in an exclusion zone for at least 24 hours.
When left unattended, the EWP's power and controls, including remote controls, are isolated and locked off, the keys are removed, and it is parked where other plant will not hit it.
Indoors, an electric EWP is used where practicable, as emissions from engine-driven EWPs can be hazardous.
Where chemicals are used from the platform, incompatible classes are not carried together, mixing is done on the ground, and only the amount needed is taken up in a sealed container.

A telehandler is used as an EWP only with a work platform approved for that model, with platform and ground controls. Fork-mounted work platforms are not used, and no one is on the platform while it travels.

Outdoors, stop in winds above the manufacturer's limit, and check for overhead power lines
The operator is trained for the platform. A high risk work licence is needed only for a boom-type platform

Check for crushing points such as soffits, beams, steelwork and services before raising or moving the platform.
The EWP is used only as a working platform, not to enter or exit a work area at height
Workers are trained in the safe use of fall arrest equipment and the emergency rescue procedures for the EWP

text: Frames are erected progressively and braced as soon as practicable. Frame towers 2 m or more high have an internal full deck no more than 2 m below the working level, or fall protection on all four sides.

Where bearers and joists are installed 2 m or more above the level below, a full false deck is provided, with no gap over 225 mm except at frame verticals, and lapped planks are secured against uplift and slipping.

Bearers are placed from a platform no more than 2 m below them, sit in U-heads (centrally where single), and are nailed or secured where a flat plate is specified. Joists are spread from a platform within 2 m.
Platforms for erecting formwork are at least 450 mm wide, such as two scaffold planks. No one works from a single plank or bearer, or climbs the framework.
Props and frames are connected with proprietary pins, never improvised bolts or reinforcing bar, are kept within their working load limit, and are not placed close to excavation edges.
Water that could wash out under the falsework is diverted away, and after adverse weather a competent person inspects the foundations before loading continues.
An existing scaffold is used to support falsework only where the scaffold designer or manufacturer permits it.

Perimeter protection screens extend at least 1 m above the finished slab, stay in place from the start of erection until soffit stripping is complete, and gaps between the screen and deck are minimised, for example with a flexible flap.
Perimeter screens are assembled and installed by workers trained by the screen supplier, and rigging work on the screens is done by a licensed rigger.
Before screens or containment netting are fixed, the formwork designer confirms the formwork can take the extra dead and wind loads, allowing for netting being heavier and less permeable when wet.
Where perimeter scaffold is the edge protection, its guardrail is at least 900 mm above the finished slab, with hop-ups where the gap to the slab exceeds 225 mm horizontally or 300 mm vertically.
Harness-based fall arrest or work positioning systems are not used as the fall control at the formwork perimeter.
Guardrails are engineered edge protection systems to AS 4994.1 rather than framing timber, with post fixings able to take the force of a worker falling into the rail.
Wherever a leading edge is left unattended, edge protection is installed, or the deck is barricaded with keep out signs.

Where there is no false deck within 2 m below, formply is laid only over at least four joists at 450 mm centres beside the worker, extending at least 1.8 m ahead, with sheets laid in front of the worker.
Deck laying starts from the perimeter scaffold or edge protection, and gaps between tableforms or deck panels left for infill strips are limited to nominally 400 mm.
A formwork-only exclusion zone behind the leading edge is marked with signs and a barrier, and other trades use the deck only once the formwork contractor has handed it over as complete.
Cantilevered bearers, joists and ply are secured against pivoting as the design sets out, and no materials are stacked on a cantilever unless it is designed for the load.
Lower parts of the deck, such as drop panels and deep beams, are built before work starts on the higher areas.

step: Load ply onto the deck while it is being laid

Plywood penetration covers are structurally graded, painted a bright colour, firmly fixed to the deck and designed for the loads. Joists at the edge of a penetration are secured so they cannot spread if someone falls on them.
Where cast-in mesh is used as back-up protection in slab penetrations, it has an aperture of 50 mm x 50 mm or smaller and can take the imposed loads.
A competent person inspects the formwork and gives clearance to load at key stages, such as before it is loaded with components, equipment or tendons, as well as before the concrete pour.

step: Monitor the formwork during the pour
text: Concrete is placed no faster than the calculated pour rate, inboard areas before cantilevers, and pumps, hoists and other equipment are not attached to the formwork unless the design allows it.

step: Monitor the formwork during the pour
text: Competent persons stay on site during the pour to make emergency adjustments or repairs, and placement stops while they are made.
Before stripping, any penetration that will be exposed is covered, and voids, shafts and stair openings are protected with rails, scaffold or secured and marked covers.
Stripped components are de-nailed before stacking, stacks do not block access ways or work areas, nothing is dropped or thrown from the structure, and task lighting is provided.
Before each climb, Z-bars, ferrule bolts and anything else that could snag on the structure are removed and signed off, and cables and water pipes are arranged so they cannot snag or rupture.
A system keeps the form level during the climb, either automated or with operators ready to stop it, and nip and shear points are identified and controlled.
A form being removed from a wall is supported so it never relies on suction or on through bolts that are about to be removed.

Each platform has a sign stating its maximum load in kilograms. Anyone on a platform while it is lifted or suspended by a crane holds a dogging or rigging licence or is supervised by someone who does.
Ladder openings in working decks have guardrails and trapdoors that stay closed except when in use. Where the access stair is designed for less than 2.5 kPa, its maximum load is signed.
Fire extinguishers are provided on the form as a competent person advises, and the tested emergency procedure covers getting workers out of every level and cell, including lift voids.
Trailing screens use heavy-duty containment netting to stop falling objects.

text: The safety observer marks the border of the no go zone near electric lines with markers such as red warning tape, stops unauthorised people entering, observes only one operating crane at a time, and has authority to stop the work.
Before use, the crane operator and dogger check the radios are dry and working, with a fully charged battery and a spare, and use a constant talk method so everyone knows the progress of the lift.
Hand signals, whistles, or bell and buzzer signals are agreed for use alongside radios or when radios are not available.
Remote controls are generally not used if the crane has a cabin. Wireless remotes are uniquely coded to avoid signal corruption and interference from other devices.

People are lifted only in a design registered work box, with harnesses attached to its anchorage points, and only where scaffolding or an elevating work platform is not reasonably practicable. The crane's free fall facility is locked out.
Fire extinguishers or a fire suppression system are readily accessible to the operator, and only necessary quantities of combustibles are stored on the machine deck.

The emergency plan covers rescue from the crane, agreed with the fire and emergency services, and where practicable a second crane driver can make the crane safe if the operator becomes incapacitated.

find: A dedicated radio frequency is used for the duration of the crane operations
Only one dogger gives signals at any time. Where more than one dogger is involved in a lift
Work stops immediately if radio communication is lost. Mobile phones are not used to direct tower crane operations.
An anemometer is fixed on the tower crane where it is not shielded from the wind
a trained safety observer (spotter) watches and advises the operator. The safety observer does not carry out dogging or other tasks at the same time.
The crane operator does not do their own dogging (for example on a remote control tower crane)
On a self-erecting or remotely operated crane, the operator works from a designated area close to the crane
If the remote control operator needs to do other tasks, the remote control is turned off and secured
A barricade about 1800 mm high (for example a mesh fence) is erected around the base of a self-erecting tower crane
Before each work shift the crane operator visually inspects and function tests the crane
Where more than one crane works, the cranes use the anti-collision or zoning system

text: Before lifting, the crane operator or dogger checks the hoist rope hangs vertically above the load and the marked load mass is correct and within the crane's rated capacity.

text: Slings are not crossed or twisted, the lift point is directly above the load's centre of gravity, and pipes, joists, timber or sheeting are strapped together and lifted flat.

text: Where plasterboard is lifted without a material box, the lifting system is certified by an engineer or an intermediate or advanced rigger, and sets the minimum and maximum number of sheets and the number, position and capacity of slings.

text: When left unattended, the crane is left to weathervane to the manufacturer's instructions, with the hook raised clear of people, plant and structures as it moves, and the power and remote controls isolated and locked off.

find: Before directing a lift, the dogger checks each sling, shackle and lifting attachment
Lifting hooks have operable safety latches, shackles are prevented from unscrewing
Round (sausage) slings are used only for round loads
Lifting gear is inspected by a competent person at least every 12 months, and synthetic slings every 3 months
after lifting the load a few centimetres the operator tests the hoist brakes
Except in an emergency, the crane operator does not leave the cabin or control room while a load is suspended
Material boxes are engineer designed and certified, marked with their tare mass and SWL
Basket hitches are not used where people may be near a lifted load
Avoid lifting multiple loads at the same time (high/low loads)

text: No signs are attached to the crane boom. Signs on the machine deck are certified by an engineer, and solid signs are bolted on, never fixed by drilling, welding, strapping or cable ties.

text: Delivered crane components are inspected for damage and wear from transport, and tower sections are permanently marked with their model and serial number, matching the registered crane design.

text: Counterweights are secured as the crane manufacturer specifies. Where a moving counterweight is latched at the top of its rail for climbing, the latch has a secondary securing means, such as a rope or chain to the machine deck.

text: During climbing, the crane's centre of gravity is balanced over the climbing equipment to the designer's, manufacturer's or engineer's balancing procedure.

step: Erect or dismantle the tower crane
text: Crane ties are installed to the crane designer's and manufacturer's instructions, and a competent person verifies the structure they are tied to can take the crane's forces.

text: Riggers on the jib use the rigger's run and static lines along the full jib, with double lanyards to stay attached when moving between jib sections.

text: On continuous vertical tower ladders, a fall-arrest system with a vertical rail or rope and locking cam device is used, so climbers do not hook on and off, with no more than 300 mm of lanyard to the rail or rope.

text: A reliable communication system links the surface and underground work areas whenever workers are underground, and is maintained and tested at regular intervals. An emergency warning system can quickly alert workers underground to evacuate.

Workers and materials are transported separately unless the system is designed for both. Walkways are clearly marked, slip-resistant, lit, free from obstructions, and have handrails or barriers where there is a risk of falling.

Excavation goes ahead under a permit to tunnel, with geological and monitoring data and support installation reviewed daily by competent personnel. Where conditions fall outside the design, pre-planned actions make the excavation safe and stop further excavation.

Scaling works systematically towards the face within a defined exclusion zone, using suitable or remotely operated plant with overhead protection, and a competent person checks scaled areas are safe before other work proceeds.
Underground plant has rollover and falling object protective structures, with FOPS Level 2 unless it is shown the plant will not be exposed to high-energy falling objects.

Operators slow to no more than walking speed and sound the horn or radio before negotiating blind spots, and workers on foot confirm by radio with the operator that it is safe before approaching plant.
Everyone is within range of the atmospheric alarms for their work area. On a Level 2 (evacuation) alarm, self-rescuers are donned where required and the tunnel is evacuated under the emergency plan.
No petrol or other volatile fuel engines go underground. Diesel engines are Tier 4 Final or EU Stage V (or equivalent), and operators minimise idling and shut engines off during idle periods.
A diesel engine whose tail pipe emissions exceed 1100 ppm carbon monoxide or 750 ppm oxides of nitrogen is taken out of service for maintenance or repair.
Welding and cutting are done at the surface, or replaced with cold processes, where practicable. A firewatcher attends during hot work and stays for at least 30 minutes after it finishes.

Everyone underground is trained to use self-contained self-rescuers and knows where they are if not carried. Where safe egress cannot be assured before the air becomes irrespirable, everyone has immediate access to an oxygen self-rescuer.

Shaft collars and openings have edge protection and barriers to stop people or materials falling in, with a signposted, barricaded exclusion zone around shaft tops, and a suitable means of hoisting injured persons from the shaft.

find: Everyone underground is tagged in and out
hot work underground is done only under a permit.

text: Where the platform operator could be trapped or crushed against the tunnel lining, services or ground support, an EWP with secondary crush protection or an anti-entrapment system is used.
Lighting gives at least 40 lux in general access ways and stairways and 160 lux for typical building work. An area that cannot be lit adequately is locked out and not used.
High intensity lights, such as halogen and metal halide fittings, are mounted high enough and angled to prevent glare and contact burns, and kept clear of combustible materials.
Toilets are provided at no less than 1 pan per 15 males (and 1 urinal per 20 males) and 1 pan per 10 females, with a means to dispose of sanitary items, and are kept clean and not used for storage.
Washbasins have hot and cold running water, soap and towels or dryers, and cool, clean drinking water is provided free of charge.
